What this speech is really normalizing is the idea that advancement isn’t about creativity, problem solving, or genuine merit it's about keeping the people above you happy. That dynamic creates a toxic hierarchy where egos become the currency of power. Sponsors aren’t just mentors; they become gatekeepers who decide whose voice matters, and unsurprisingly, they tend to reward those who flatter them rather than those who challenge them. In such systems, cliques of self important leaders gang up to protect their own status. They elevate sycophants who echo their views, while sidelining independent thinkers who bring fresh, tangential ideas. The result is an echo chamber: innovation is stifled, dissent is punished, and the organization becomes more concerned with loyalty than with solving real problems. Toxic hierarchies thrive on fear and dependency. People learn quickly that survival means appeasing the powerful, not questioning them. Over time, the hierarchy becomes less about competence and more about politics who you know, who you please, and who you avoid offending. And ironically, the very people most capable of creative breakthroughs are often the ones pushed out, because their refusal to play the sycophancy game threatens the fragile egos at the top.
